::: {.callout-note}
## How to use this tutorial
This tutorial turns the [lecture](../l_08_LiteratureReviews.qmd) into eight
steps you carry out yourself. Each step points back to the lecture chapter that
explains the *why*; here we focus on the *how*.

- **Example topic:** the four-day week and other forms of working time
  reduction. It is deliberately *not* the topic of the take-home examination.
  Use it to practise, then repeat the steps on your own topic.
- **Database:** [OpenAlex](https://openalex.org) — free, open, and the same for
  everyone. Everything in the main steps works without any paid subscription.
- **Templates:** download the
  [workbook with all templates](L08-review-templates.xlsx) (search log,
  screening sheet, concept matrix, limitations). It works in Excel, LibreOffice
  and Numbers.
- **Digression:** [a second database](#sec-second) —
  [EconBiz](#sec-econbiz), the free subject portal for economics, and what
  [Web of Science](#sec-wos) adds if you have access through a university.
- **Optional R part:** [the R part](#sec-r) runs the whole search from R, which makes it fully
  reproducible. The code is shown but not run on this page, because it needs
  your own (free) API key. The complete example, with all results, is available
  via the repo [RM-LitReviewTutorial](https://github.com/graebnerc/RM-LitReviewTutorial) on GitHub.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## Hit counts will differ
OpenAlex is updated continuously. Your numbers will not match anyone else's
exactly — which is why you record the **date** and the **exact query** of every
search, and why the R part saves a copy of each result set.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## The illustration matters
This tutorial is meant to mimic a complete review. But you can easily follow
the steps by just doing a reduced version. This might be more time-efficient
if you just want to get an idea of how to do such a review.
:::

# Step 1: From topic to question and concept table

*Lecture chapter 2.*

A topic is not a question. Start by writing a question that tells you what is
in and what is out:

> **Example question:** *Which effects of reducing working time — in particular
> through a four-day week — on employees and firms are reported in empirical
> studies?*

This is an effects question, so it follows the **PICO** format: 

- **p**opulation — employees and firms; 
- **i**ntervention — working time reduction; 
- **c**omparison — regular working hours; 
- **o**utcome — productivity, well-being and the like. 

A question that maps what is known
about a topic rather than an effect should follow **PCC** instead: population,
concept, context. Population and comparison usually end up in your inclusion
criteria, intervention and outcome become the concepts of your search.

Then split the question into its **concepts** and collect, for each concept,
the different ways in which authors express it. One column per concept:

| Working time reduction | Outcomes | (Empirical design) |
|:-----------------------|:---------|:-------------------|
| four-day week, 4-day week | productivity, productive | trial |
| working time reduction, work time reduction | well-being, wellbeing | survey |
| reduced working hours | job satisfaction | panel |
| shorter working week, shorter workweek | burnout, stress | case study |
| compressed work week ⚠️ | absenteeism, turnover | |

: Example concept table. The third column is optional: you can capture "empirical" through the string or through your inclusion criteria — but you must document which.

OpenAlex finds plural forms automatically (stemming), but not spelling variants
or related word forms. List them explicitly: *well-being* and *wellbeing*,
*labor* and *labour*, *productivity* and *productive*.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## ⚠️ Same words, different interventions
A *compressed* work week usually means the **same** number of hours in fewer
days. A four-day week in the "100-80-100" sense means **fewer** hours for the
same pay. Both are called "four-day week" in parts of the literature. Decide now
whether both are in scope — and write it into your criteria. This is the
terminology problem from lecture chapter 6 in miniature: the same word can name
different things, and different words can name the same thing.
:::

**Write down your inclusion and exclusion criteria now**, before you search.
For the example:

- **Include:** empirical studies (quantitative or qualitative) of a reduction
  in working time at firm, sector or country level that report at least one
  outcome for employees or firms.
- **Exclude:** purely conceptual or normative papers; studies of part-time work
  chosen by individuals; overtime regulation without reduction of normal hours.
- **Document type:** journal articles and reviews.
- **Language:** English (a limitation you will report in Step 8).
- **Period:** no restriction.

# Step 2: Harvest terms and build a test set

*Lecture chapter 3.*

Your concept table is only as good as your vocabulary. Three sources help:

1. **Key papers you already know.** Look at their titles, abstracts and author
   keywords. Every term they use belongs in your table.
2. **A semantic search tool** (see the
   [tool list in lecture 2](../l_02_AITools.qmd#b-grounded-search)). Ask it your
   question, then look at the *vocabulary* of the papers it suggests — not at
   its summary.
3. **Neighbouring communities.** Who else works on this? Labour economists,
   occupational health researchers, management scholars, and degrowth and
   ecological economists all study working time — with different words
   ("working time reduction", "work-sharing", "sufficiency").

At the same time, build a **test set**: three to five papers (a stand-alone
review uses five to ten) that *must* be
found by a good search. Note them, with their DOIs, in the search log.

::: {.callout-important}
## Put closed-access papers into your test set
Include at least one or two papers from **closed-access journals of large
publishers** (Elsevier, Springer Nature). Many of these have no abstract in
OpenAlex (lecture chapter 3). If your string misses them, you know that the
missing abstracts are costing you recall — and you might need to compensate 
for that in Step 6.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## Verify what AI tools suggest
Any paper a semantic tool suggests must be found in OpenAlex or opened at the
publisher before it enters your test set. A paper that you cannot find anywhere
does not exist (see the [citation-checking exercise](../ai-citation-check/index.qmd)).
:::

# Step 3: Build and test the search string in OpenAlex

*Lecture chapter 3.*

## Translate the table into a string

OR within a concept, AND between concepts:

| Element | Syntax | Note |
|:--------|:-------|:-----|
| Operators | `AND`, `OR`, `NOT` | Must be in **capitals** |
| Phrases | `"working time reduction"` | Double quotation marks |
| Grouping | `( … ) AND ( … )` | Parentheses set the order |
| Word forms | — | Plurals are found automatically (stemming); spelling variants and related forms must be listed |
| Wildcards | — | Not available in the web interface; list the variants instead |

: OpenAlex search syntax in brief. Check the [OpenAlex help pages](https://help.openalex.org) for the current rules.

A first version of the example string:

```text
("four-day week" OR "four day week" OR "4-day week" OR "four-day workweek"
 OR "working time reduction" OR "work time reduction"
 OR "reduced working hours" OR "reduction in working hours"
 OR "shorter working week" OR "shorter workweek")
AND
(productivity OR productive OR "well-being" OR wellbeing OR satisfaction
 OR burnout OR stress OR absenteeism OR turnover OR performance)
```

## Run it in the web interface

::: {.callout-note}
## Other ways to run the same search
The web interface is the easiest route, and the one this step describes. The
same string also works in other ways:

- **R**, with the package openalexR: [the R part](#sec-r) below, and a
  complete project that reproduces the whole example (see there). Your script
  then *is* your search documentation.
- **Python**, with the package [pyalex](https://github.com/J535D165/pyalex).
- **The API directly**: a search is a web address, e.g.
  `https://api.openalex.org/works?filter=title_and_abstract.search:"four-day week"`
  — paste it into your browser and you get the answer as data (JSON).
- **Another database** with the same concepts: EconBiz or Web of Science —
  see [the digression](#sec-second).

Routes through the API (R, Python, web address) need a free OpenAlex API key
for anything beyond the first page of results.
:::

1. Go to [openalex.org](https://openalex.org) and paste the string into the
   search field.
2. Restrict the search to **title and abstract** if the interface offers this
   option. The default search also looks into the full text of those works for
   which OpenAlex has one — which makes the result depend on which papers happen
   to be open access.
3. Add filters for **year**, **type** (article, review) and **language**.
   Language tags in OpenAlex are not always correct; check a sample of what
   the filter removes.
4. Note the number of results, and **copy the page address (URL)** into your
   search log: it contains your full query and all filters.

::: {.callout-note}
## Interfaces change
Web interfaces are redesigned regularly. If a button described here has moved,
the logic stays the same: one query, explicit filters, a documented result. The
[R part](#sec-r) runs exactly the same search through the API and is not affected
by interface changes.
:::

## Test recall with your test set

Search for each test-set paper by title or DOI. Is it in your result set? If a
paper is missing, look at it in OpenAlex:

- **It has an abstract** → your string lacks a term. Find the term in its
  title or abstract, add it, rerun, and **log the new version**.
- **It has no abstract** → only its title could have matched. Is there a term
  that authors in this field typically put into *titles*? Add it. Otherwise,
  note the paper — Step 6 will have to catch papers like it.

# Step 4: Keep a search log

*Lecture chapter 7.*

The search log is what makes your review reproducible. Use the sheet
**Search log** in the [template workbook](L08-review-templates.xlsx). For every
version of your string, record:

| Field | Example |
|:------|:--------|
| Date | 2026-11-12 |
| Database and route | OpenAlex, web interface (or: API via R) |
| Version of your string | v2 — you number your string versions yourself |
| Full string | `( … ) AND ( … )` — copied, not paraphrased |
| Search field | Title and abstract |
| Filters | Type: article, review; language: English |
| Results | number of records |
| Query URL / script | the page URL, or the name of your R script |
| Test set found | e.g. 4 of 5 |
| Share without abstract | e.g. 0.18 — share of the results without abstract |
| Change from previous version | added "work-sharing" after test paper 3 was missed |

: What goes into the search log.

The **version** is that of *your search string*, not of OpenAlex: every time
you change the string, give it a new number (v1, v2, …), so that you can say
which version found what. OpenAlex itself has no version number you could
cite; the **date** of the search takes its place.

::: {.callout-note}
A string you cannot reproduce from your log is a string you cannot report. Fill
in the log *while* you search, not afterwards.
:::

# Step 5: Export, fill in missing abstracts, and screen

*Lecture chapter 4.*

## Export

Use the **export** function of the web interface and choose the spreadsheet
format (CSV). Keep this file untouched as the record of your search, and work
on a copy. Alternatively, let R fetch the records and build the screening sheet
([in R](#sec-r-screening)). For writing, you can additionally export in RIS format for
Zotero.

## Fill in missing abstracts

Before screening, sort your records by whether they have an abstract. For every
record without one:

1. **Open the publisher's page through the DOI** (`https://doi.org/` followed by
   the DOI). Abstracts are free to read there, even for articles behind a
   paywall — they are only missing from OpenAlex because publishers do not allow
   their redistribution (lecture chapter 6).
2. If the publisher page does not help, look for an **open-access version**:
   OpenAlex links to repository copies where it knows them, and many working
   papers are on SSRN, RePEc or the authors' websites.
3. Copy the abstract into the screening sheet and record **where** it came from
   (column `abstract_source`).

The R part can fill in some abstracts automatically from Crossref
([in R](#sec-r-abstracts)) — but not those of publishers that do not deposit abstracts
there, which includes Elsevier and Springer Nature.

## Screen titles and abstracts

Use the sheet **Screening** in the template workbook — one row per record. For
each record:

- **decision_ta:** include / exclude / unsure (unsure stays in for round 2)
- **reason_ta:** optional at this stage

## Screen full texts

For every record that survived round 1, read the full text and decide:

- **decision_ft:** include / exclude / not retrievable
- **reason_ft:** **required** for every exclusion — use a short, fixed list of
  reasons (e.g. *not empirical*, *no working-time reduction*, *no outcome
  reported*)

::: {.callout-tip}
## Ask someone to screen a sample
Exchange 20 records with a fellow student and screen each other's sample blind.
Where you disagree, your criteria are not yet precise enough. Sharpen them, and
note the change in the search log.
:::

## How far do two screeners agree? Cohen's kappa {#sec-kappa}

When two people screen the same records independently, report how far they
agree. The share of identical decisions flatters: most records are easy
exclusions, so two screeners agree often by chance alone. **Cohen's kappa** ($\kappa$)
corrects for this [@cohen1960coefficient].

Take the records that both screened, compare their decisions (in the workbook:
`decision_ta` and *Screener 2 (sample)*), and count the four combinations.
Treat *unsure* as *include*, because both go on to round 2. An example with
100 records:

|                       | Screener B: include | Screener B: exclude |
|:----------------------|:-------------------:|:-------------------:|
| **Screener A: include** |      15 (*a*)     |       5 (*b*)       |
| **Screener A: exclude** |      10 (*c*)     |      70 (*d*)       |

1. **Observed agreement:** $p_o = \frac{a + d}{N} = \frac{85}{100} = 0.85$
2. **Agreement expected by chance**, from how often each screener says include
   and exclude:
   $p_e = \frac{a+b}{N} \cdot \frac{a+c}{N} + \frac{c+d}{N} \cdot \frac{b+d}{N} = 0.20 \cdot 0.25 + 0.80 \cdot 0.75 = 0.65$
3. **Kappa:** $\kappa = \frac{p_o - p_e}{1 - p_e} = \frac{0.85 - 0.65}{1 - 0.65} \approx 0.57$

So 85% agreement is only a kappa of 0.57. A value of 0 means no better than
chance and 1 means perfect agreement. A common rough convention calls 0.41–0.60
*moderate*, 0.61–0.80 *substantial* and anything above that *almost perfect*
[@landis1977measurement]. With few records, kappa is unstable, so always report
the counts as well, and say how the disagreements were resolved.

# Step 6: Snowball from your best papers — compulsory

*Lecture chapter 3.*

Snowballing is optional in many review guides. **Here it is compulsory**,
because it compensates for the missing abstracts: citation links do not depend
on abstracts, so it finds exactly those papers that a title-and-abstract search
could not see.

Choose two or three included papers that fit your question best — ideally
including one from a closed-access journal. Choose them for their fit, not for
their citation counts: in the [companion project](https://github.com/graebnerc/RM-LitReviewTutorial), the
most-cited hit of the example search was a paper on the economic burden of
dementia, and snowballing from it returned hundreds of medical papers and none
of the test papers. Two included papers on working time, by contrast, reached
a test paper that the string had missed. In OpenAlex, open each record:

- **Backward:** its **references** — the papers it builds on.
- **Forward:** **cited by** — papers that build on it.

Screen what you find **with the same criteria**, and count the snowballed
papers separately; they get their own box in the flow diagram. If there are
more records than you can screen, narrow them down in a documented way — for
example with a title filter that keeps only records whose title mentions your
intervention — and report it. In R,
`oa_snowball()` does both directions in one call ([in R](#sec-r-snowball)).

::: {.callout-warning}
## Snowballing stays inside the community
Papers that cite each other share a vocabulary and often a perspective.
Snowballing is good at finding what your keywords missed *within* that
community, and bad at finding the community next door. That is why it
complements the string search and never replaces it.
:::

# Step 7: Fill the concept matrix and synthesise

*Lecture chapter 5.*

Before reading the included papers in depth, fix the **columns** of your
extraction sheet. Use the sheet **Concept matrix** in the template workbook.
For the example:

| Column | What you record |
|:-------|:----------------|
| Intervention | Reduced hours (e.g. 100-80-100) / compressed week / other |
| Context | Country, sector, firm size |
| Design | Trial, survey, panel, case study, … |
| Selection | How did firms or employees get into the study? |
| Outcomes | Which outcomes, measured how? |
| Findings | Direction, size, conditions |
| Caveats | What makes you trust the study more or less? |

: Example columns of the concept matrix.

Pilot the columns on three papers, adjust them once, then keep them fixed.
A filled matrix could look like this:

| Study | Intervention | Context | Design | Selection | Outcomes | Findings | Caveats |
|:------|:-------------|:--------|:-------|:----------|:---------|:---------|:--------|
| A | Reduced hours, 100-80-100 | UK, mixed sectors, small firms | Pilot, survey before and after | Firms volunteered | Burnout, job satisfaction (self-reported) | Burnout down, satisfaction up | No control group; self-selected firms |
| B | Shorter legal workweek | One country, all sectors | Panel, before and after a law | Everyone covered by the law | Job and leisure satisfaction | Small rise in satisfaction | A policy change, not a four-day week |
| C | Compressed week: same hours in four days | US, one manufacturing plant | Case study over a year | One plant | Fatigue, satisfaction | Early enthusiasm, fatigue later | One firm; long working days |

: Example concept matrix (illustrative studies, not real ones).

Reading the column *Intervention* already changes the picture: A and C are
both called a "four-day week", but A cuts hours and C only rearranges them —
so their different findings on fatigue are no contradiction.

Then **read the matrix by column**: Where do studies agree? Where do they
disagree — and does the disagreement line up with intervention type, design or
context? That is your synthesis. Write it as a paragraph organised by these
patterns, not as one summary per paper.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## A bias to watch for in this example
Firms that volunteer for a four-day-week trial are not a random sample of
firms. Some of the evidence also comes from organisations that campaign for
working time reduction, and appears as reports rather than journal articles.
Neither is a reason to exclude the evidence — both are things to record in the
*Selection* and *Caveats* columns and to discuss in your limitations.
:::

# Step 8: Draw the flow diagram and report

*Lecture chapters 4 and 7.*

## The flow diagram

Count what happened to every record:

| Box | From |
|:----|:-----|
| Records identified | Search log, final version |
| Records screened / excluded | Screening sheet, round 1 |
| Reports sought / not retrievable | Screening sheet, round 2 |
| Reports assessed / excluded with reasons | Screening sheet, round 2 |
| Records from other sources | Snowballing |
| Studies included | Concept matrix |

: Where the numbers for the flow diagram come from.

![The PRISMA 2020 flow diagram of the example review, drawn in R with the
PRISMA2020 package from the companion project (search of 7 November 2026). The
left column follows the records from OpenAlex to the included studies; the
boxes next to it show what dropped out at each stage, with reasons; the right
arm adds the studies found by snowballing — of the 205 new records, only the
44 whose title mentions working time were sought. Click to enlarge.](prisma-tutorial.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="PRISMA 2020 flow diagram: 411 records identified from OpenAlex, 11 duplicates removed, 400 screened, 323 excluded; 77 reports sought, 6 not retrieved; 71 assessed, 35 excluded (no reduction in working time 29, no outcome for employees or firms 3, not in English 2, not empirical 1). Snowballing: 205 records identified, 44 sought, 2 not retrieved, 42 assessed, 29 excluded. 49 studies included."}

The screening behind this diagram was done by an AI assistant as a
demonstration, on titles and abstracts only, and was not checked by a person
— a limitation that the example paragraphs below have to report, and that
your own review should avoid.

Draw it with the [PRISMA2020 Shiny app](https://estech.shinyapps.io/prisma_flowdiagram/),
the templates on the [PRISMA website](https://www.prisma-statement.org/), or
[in R](#sec-r-prisma).

## The methods paragraph

In a term paper, the following fits into one paragraph plus an appendix:

1. Database, route (web interface or API) and date of the search
2. The full final string and all filters (appendix), plus the query URL or script
3. Inclusion and exclusion criteria
4. How missing abstracts were handled
5. Who screened, how far screeners agreed ([Cohen's kappa](#sec-kappa)), and how
   disagreements were handled
6. The numbers → flow diagram
7. How you synthesised (concept matrix, which dimensions)

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Example: a methods paragraph
*(The numbers are those of the flow diagram above.)*

> We searched OpenAlex on 7 November 2026 through its API (R package
> openalexR), in titles and abstracts, for articles and reviews in English
> (full string and script in Appendix A). We included empirical studies,
> quantitative or qualitative, of an actual reduction in working time at
> firm, sector or country level that report at least one outcome for
> employees or firms; conceptual papers, models, reviews, compressed work
> weeks and individually chosen part-time work were excluded. Of the 411
> records, 41 (10 %) had no abstract in OpenAlex, most of them closed-access
> articles from Elsevier and Springer Nature; Crossref provided none of these
> abstracts. After removing 11 duplicates, the titles and abstracts of 400
> records were screened, and 77 were assessed against the criteria. Screening
> was carried out by an AI assistant (Claude) as a demonstration, on titles
> and abstracts only, and was not checked by a person; six records could not
> be assessed without their full text. Backward and forward snowballing from
> two included studies identified 205 further records, of which the 44 whose
> titles mention working time were screened with the same criteria. Of the
> 49 included studies (36 from the search, 13 from snowballing), we would
> extract intervention, context, design, selection, outcomes and findings
> into a concept matrix (Appendix B) and synthesise them by intervention type
> and design (Figure 1).
:::

## The limitations paragraph

Use the sheet **Limitations** in the template workbook. For each limitation,
name **the bias**, **its likely direction**, and **why you accepted it**.

> *Generic:* "Some relevant studies may have been missed."
>
> *Specific:* "The search covered titles and abstracts in OpenAlex. Of the
> 411 records, 41 had no abstract, most of them closed-access articles from
> Elsevier and Springer Nature; for such records only titles can match, so
> the true gap is larger. One of our four test papers — a 1973 study without
> an abstract whose title contains no outcome term — was found neither by
> the string nor by snowballing. Snowballing from two included studies added
> 13 studies, among them a closed-access test paper the string had missed,
> but some recall loss for closed-access articles remains likely. Screening
> was done by an AI assistant on titles and abstracts only and was not
> checked by a person, so misclassifications in both directions are likely.
> Restricting the review to English excludes the German-language literature
> on *Arbeitszeitverkürzung* — EconBiz alone lists 811 records — which
> probably under-represents studies of collective working-time agreements."

Do not forget the [AI disclosure](../ai-disclosure/index.qmd) if you used AI at
any step.

# Digression: a second database {#sec-second}

No database covers everything (lecture chapter 6), so many reviews search a
second one. This digression shows two options: **EconBiz**, which is free and
open like OpenAlex, and **Web of Science**, which needs a subscription.

## EconBiz: the subject portal for economics {#sec-econbiz}

[EconBiz](https://www.econbiz.de) [@zbw2026econbiz] is the search portal of the
ZBW, the Leibniz Information Centre for Economics. A single search covers the
ZBW catalogue ECONIS, the open-access repository EconStor, RePEc working
papers and further sources. It is free and needs no account.

**What it adds:**

- **Books, edited volumes and working papers:** in our example, about half of
  the records are books or reports rather than journal articles.
- **German-language literature:** the search
  `Arbeitszeitverkürzung OR "Vier-Tage-Woche" OR "4-Tage-Woche"` returned
  about 800 records on 28 October 2026, most of them in German — exactly the
  literature our example limitations paragraph had to exclude.
- **Subject terms:** records carry ZBW subject terms in German and English, so
  a search can also match records via their subject terms (`subject:`), not
  only via the words their authors chose.

**What it lacks:**

- **No abstracts in the results.** Abstracts are *searched*, but the results
  do not show them. For screening, follow the link to EconStor, which shows the
  abstract ([in R](#sec-r-second)), or to the publisher, or look up the DOI in
  OpenAlex.
- **No citation data:** backward and forward snowballing (step 6) stays in
  OpenAlex.
- **Fewer DOIs:** in our example, fewer than half of the records have one, so
  you cannot match records with OpenAlex by DOI alone.
- **Duplicates within EconBiz:** the same work often comes from two sources
  (e.g. ECONIS and EconStor), with slightly different titles. Remove duplicates
  before you screen.
- **Economics and business only:** for neighbouring disciplines, such as
  psychology or sociology, its coverage is thin.

**Search syntax:** fields are addressed as `field:(terms)`. Abstracts sit in
**two different fields**, depending on the source: `abstract` (mainly
EconStor) and `description` (mainly the ZBW catalogue). Search both: either
field alone finds only about half of the records with a matching abstract. Phrase search (`"four-day week"`), truncation
(`productiv*`) and `AND`/`OR`/`NOT` with brackets work as in OpenAlex. The
example string, searching titles, abstracts and descriptions:

```text
(title:(W) OR abstract:(W) OR description:(W))
AND
(title:(O) OR abstract:(O) OR description:(O))

W = "four-day week" OR "4-day week" OR "four day week"
    OR "working time reduction" OR "work time reduction"
    OR "reduced working hours" OR "shorter working week"
O = productiv* OR well-being OR wellbeing OR satisfaction
    OR burnout OR stress OR absentee* OR turnover OR performance
```

Write out `W` and `O` in full when you search; [the R part](#sec-r-second) builds the string
in R. On 28 October 2026 it returned 98 records, and 74 after events and duplicates
were removed.

## Web of Science: what a paid database adds {#sec-wos}

If you have access to **Web of Science** through a university, it is worth
seeing what a curated, commercial database does differently — and what that
costs.

**What it adds:**

- **Precise search syntax:** field tags (`TS=` for title, abstract and
  keywords; `TI=` for titles only), truncation (`productiv*`) and wildcards
  (`organi?ation`), and proximity operators.
- **Search history:** run each concept as its own search (`#1`, `#2`) and
  combine them (`#1 AND #2`) — you see how much each concept contributes.
- **Abstracts** for nearly all indexed journal articles.
- **Curated journal selection** and consistent metadata.

**What it costs:**

- **Money and access:** an institutional subscription. Access depends on the
  contract of your university, differs between institutions — which also means
  that others may not be able to rerun your search — and ends when you leave.
- **Coverage:** fewer books, working papers, non-English and Global South
  publications than OpenAlex (lecture chapter 6).

The example string in Web of Science syntax:

```text
TS=("four-day week*" OR "4-day week*" OR "four day week*"
    OR "working time reduction" OR "work time reduction"
    OR "reduced working hours" OR "shorter working week*")
AND
TS=(productiv* OR well-being OR wellbeing OR satisfaction
    OR burnout OR stress OR absentee* OR turnover OR performance)
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Exercise: compare two databases
Run the equivalent string in OpenAlex and in EconBiz — or in Web of Science, if
you have access — and compare the result sets ([in R](#sec-r-second)).
Which records does only one of them find? What kinds of publication, which
languages, which journals or series are they? This makes the coverage and
metadata biases of lecture chapter 6 visible on your own topic.
:::

# Optional: the whole search in R {#sec-r}

This part builds on the implementation lab sessions on
[importing data](/content/material/s_06_DataImport.qmd),
[data preparation](/content/material/s_07_DataPreparation.qmd) and
[visualisation](/content/material/s_08_Visualization.qmd). It uses the package
[openalexR](https://docs.ropensci.org/openalexR/) [@aria2024openalexr] to run
the search directly against the OpenAlex API. The big advantage: your script
*is* your search documentation — anyone can rerun it.

::: {.callout-note}
## The complete project
All code of this part, for the example search, is also available as one
complete project, [**RM-LitReviewTutorial**](https://github.com/graebnerc/RM-LitReviewTutorial) on GitHub: a Quarto
report that runs every step and saves every search result in its `data/`
folder. Rendering it again reads the saved results instead of searching again
— so it reproduces exactly, without an API key. Use it to see what the code
below produces, or as a starting point for your own project: download it with
*Code → Download ZIP* on GitHub, open `RM-LitReviewTutorial.Rproj`, run
`renv::restore()` once, and render `report.qmd`.
:::

## Setup and API key

OpenAlex requires a free API key for programmatic access. Create an account at
[openalex.org](https://openalex.org) and copy your key from the account
settings. Then store it **outside your scripts**, so that you never share it by
accident: open your `.Renviron` file with `usethis::edit_r_environ()` and add a
line

```text
OPENALEX_KEY=your-key-here
```

Restart R. In your script:

```{r}
here::i_am("R/review.R")
library(here)
library(openalexR)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(readr)
library(purrr)
library(stringr)
library(ggplot2)
library(httr2)

options(openalexR.apikey = Sys.getenv("OPENALEX_KEY"))
```

Without a key, all requests from your network share a small daily budget,
longer Boolean strings such as the one below are often refused with "Rate
limit exceeded … Your query uses … boolean operators", and fetching more than
one page of results is refused altogether. If you see such an error, check
that `nzchar(Sys.getenv("OPENALEX_KEY"))` returns `TRUE` (this does not print
the key itself).

## Run the search

Write the string exactly as in the web interface. Avoid commas inside the
string: the API uses commas to separate filters.

```{r}
query <- '("four-day week" OR "four day week" OR "4-day week"
  OR "four-day workweek" OR "working time reduction" OR "work time reduction"
  OR "reduced working hours" OR "reduction in working hours"
  OR "shorter working week" OR "shorter workweek")
  AND (productivity OR productive OR "well-being" OR wellbeing OR satisfaction
  OR burnout OR stress OR absenteeism OR turnover OR performance)'
query <- str_squish(query) # one line, single spaces

# First only count the hits: cheap, and good for comparing string versions
n_hits <- oa_fetch(
  entity = "works",
  title_and_abstract.search = query,
  type = c("article", "review"),
  language = "en",
  count_only = TRUE
)
n_hits$count
```

The answer also shows how OpenAlex read your string: `n_hits$x_query$oql`
puts `stemmed` before every term — stemming is switched on automatically.

When the count is plausible, fetch the records and **save a dated copy**.
OpenAlex changes over time; your saved copy is the result you report.

```{r}
works <- oa_fetch(
  entity = "works",
  title_and_abstract.search = query,
  type = c("article", "review"),
  language = "en"
)

dir.create(here("data"), showWarnings = FALSE)
write_rds(works, here("data", str_c("openalex_", Sys.Date(), ".rds")))
nrow(works)
```

## Check the test set

The four papers of the example's test set; replace them with your own.

```{r}
test_set <- tibble(
  paper = c("Lepinteur, Labour Economics",
            "Mullens & Laurijssen, BMC Public Health",
            "Raposo & van Ours, Economics Letters",
            "Nord & Costigan, Journal of Applied Psychology"),
  doi = c("10.1016/j.labeco.2018.05.010",
          "10.1186/s12889-024-19161-x",
          "10.1016/j.econlet.2009.10.001",
          "10.1037/h0035419")
)
clean_doi <- function(x) str_to_lower(str_remove(x, "^https://doi.org/"))

test_set |>
  mutate(found = doi %in% clean_doi(works$doi))
```

## Measure the abstract gap

How many of your hits have no abstract — and where are they concentrated?

```{r}
works <- works |>
  mutate(no_abstract = is.na(abstract) | abstract == "")

works |>
  summarise(records = n(), share_no_abstract = mean(no_abstract))

works |>
  group_by(host_organization_name) |>
  summarise(records = n(), share_no_abstract = round(mean(no_abstract), 2)) |>
  arrange(desc(records)) |>
  head(10)

works |>
  group_by(publication_year) |>
  summarise(share = mean(no_abstract)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = publication_year, y = share)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "Publication year", y = "Share of records without abstract",
       title = "Where the title-and-abstract search is effectively title-only") +
  theme_minimal()
```

These numbers belong in your limitations paragraph.

## Describe the result set

```{r}
# Records per year
works |>
  count(publication_year) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = publication_year, y = n)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "Publication year", y = "Records") +
  theme_minimal()

# Journals and languages
works |> count(source_display_name, sort = TRUE) |> head(15)
works |> count(language, sort = TRUE)
```

If almost everything comes from a handful of journals of one field, your
string may be speaking only one community's language.

## Compare two search strings

Terminology bias becomes visible when you compare strings built from different
vocabularies, e.g. one with only "four-day week" terms and the full string,
which adds "working time reduction" terms:

```{r}
string_a <- '("four-day week" OR "four day week" OR "4-day week")
  AND (productivity OR productive OR "well-being" OR wellbeing OR satisfaction
  OR burnout OR stress OR absenteeism OR turnover OR performance)'

works_a <- oa_fetch(
  entity = "works",
  title_and_abstract.search = str_squish(string_a),
  type = c("article", "review"),
  language = "en"
)

only_full <- setdiff(works$id, works_a$id)
length(only_full)

works |>
  filter(id %in% only_full) |>
  select(publication_year, source_display_name, title) |>
  head(20)
```

Read the titles that only the full string finds. This is the most direct way
to see what a single vocabulary would have cost you.

## Build the screening sheet {#sec-r-screening}

```{r}
screening <- works |>
  transmute(
    id, doi, publication_year, title, source_display_name, abstract,
    abstract_source = if_else(no_abstract, "", "OpenAlex"),
    decision_ta = "", reason_ta = "",
    decision_ft = "", reason_ft = "", notes = ""
  ) |>
  arrange(abstract_source) # records without abstract first

dir.create(here("output"), showWarnings = FALSE)
write_excel_csv(screening, here("output", "screening_sheet.csv"))
```

`write_excel_csv()` writes a CSV file that Excel opens with the right
encoding, so that umlauts and dashes survive.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Excel shows everything in one column?
Excel with German settings expects semicolons as separators. Write the file
with `write_excel_csv2()` instead, and read it back with `read_csv2()`.
:::

## Fill in abstracts from Crossref {#sec-r-abstracts}

Some publishers deposit abstracts with Crossref, the DOI registration agency.
The function below asks Crossref for each record without an abstract.
Elsevier and Springer Nature do not deposit abstracts there — and their
journals are where most abstracts are missing — so for them you still need
the publisher page.

```{r}
crossref_abstract <- function(doi) {
  res <- tryCatch(
    request(str_c("https://api.crossref.org/works/", clean_doi(doi))) |>
      req_perform() |>
      resp_body_json(),
    error = function(e) NULL # no record or no access: NULL
  )
  ab <- res$message$abstract
  if (is.null(ab)) NA_character_ else str_squish(str_remove_all(ab, "<[^>]+>"))
}

crossref <- screening |>
  filter(abstract_source == "", !is.na(doi)) |>
  transmute(id, crossref = map_chr(doi, \(d) {
    Sys.sleep(0.2) # be polite to the API
    crossref_abstract(d)
  }))

screening <- screening |>
  left_join(crossref, by = "id") |>
  mutate(
    abstract_source = if_else(!is.na(crossref), "Crossref", abstract_source),
    abstract = coalesce(crossref, abstract)
  ) |>
  select(-crossref)

screening |> count(abstract_source)
write_excel_csv(screening, here("output", "screening_sheet.csv"))
```

Everything still without an abstract: open the DOI link (OpenAlex stores DOIs as
links) and copy the abstract from the publisher page by hand, setting
`abstract_source` to "publisher page".

## Snowball {#sec-r-snowball}

`oa_snowball()` collects, for your seed papers, both the papers they cite and
the papers that cite them:

```{r}
seeds <- c("W0000000001", "W0000000002") # OpenAlex IDs of your seed papers

snow <- oa_snowball(identifier = seeds)

# Only what the string search has not already found
short_id <- function(x) str_remove(x, ".*/")
new <- snow$nodes |>
  filter(!oa_input, !short_id(id) %in% short_id(works$id))
nrow(new)
```

Screen the new records with the same criteria and count them separately for
the flow diagram. Snowballing from highly cited papers can return thousands of
records; then narrow them down in a documented way, e.g. with a title filter
(as in the companion project) or by restricting it to the papers your seeds
cite (backward) plus recent citing papers.

## Draw the flow diagram {#sec-r-prisma}

Once screening is done, read the completed sheet back in:

```{r}
screened <- read_csv(here("output", "screening_sheet.csv"),
                     col_types = cols(.default = col_character()))

screened |> count(decision_ta)
screened |> filter(decision_ta != "exclude") |> count(decision_ft)
screened |> filter(decision_ft == "exclude") |> count(reason_ft, sort = TRUE)
```

The [PRISMA2020](https://cran.r-project.org/package=PRISMA2020) package
[@haddaway2022prisma2020] draws the diagram from a template that ships with the
package. Install it once with `install.packages("PRISMA2020")`. The column
`data` names each box and the column `n` holds its number:

```{r}
library(PRISMA2020)

template <- read_csv(system.file("extdata", "PRISMA.csv", package = "PRISMA2020"),
                     col_types = cols(.default = col_character()))
template |> select(data, description, n)
```

The small helper below sets one number and stops with an error if a box name is
misspelled — otherwise a typo would silently leave the template value in your
diagram.

```{r}
set_n <- function(tab, field, value) {
  if (!field %in% tab$data) stop("Unknown box in PRISMA template: ", field)
  tab |> mutate(n = if_else(data == field, as.character(value), n))
}
```

Most numbers come straight from the completed screening sheet; only the
snowballing numbers are entered by hand (the ones below are **illustrative**).
Exclusion reasons are passed as `"reason, n; reason, n"`.

```{r}
# Database arm: computed from the screening sheet
sought        <- screened |> filter(decision_ta != "exclude") |> nrow()
not_retrieved <- screened |> filter(decision_ft == "not retrievable") |> nrow()
reasons       <- screened |> filter(decision_ft == "exclude") |> count(reason_ft)
included_db   <- screened |> filter(decision_ft == "include") |> nrow()

# Snowballing arm: entered by hand (illustrative numbers)
snowball_found    <- 9
snowball_included <- 6

counts <- list(
  database_results           = nrow(screened),
  duplicates                 = 0,
  records_screened           = nrow(screened),
  records_excluded           = screened |> filter(decision_ta == "exclude") |> nrow(),
  dbr_sought_reports         = sought,
  dbr_notretrieved_reports   = not_retrieved,
  dbr_assessed               = sought - not_retrieved,
  dbr_excluded               = str_c(reasons$reason_ft, ", ", reasons$n,
                                     collapse = "; "),
  citations_results          = snowball_found,
  other_sought_reports       = snowball_found,
  other_notretrieved_reports = 0,
  other_assessed             = snowball_found,
  other_excluded             = str_c("Not eligible, ",
                                     snowball_found - snowball_included),
  new_studies                = included_db + snowball_included,
  new_reports                = included_db + snowball_included
)

for (box in names(counts)) {
  template <- set_n(template, box, counts[[box]])
}

flow <- PRISMA_data(as.data.frame(template))
PRISMA_flowdiagram(flow, previous = FALSE, other = TRUE, fontsize = 12)
```

`other = TRUE` draws the right-hand arm for snowballing; `previous = FALSE`
hides the arm for earlier versions of a review, which you do not have.

## Compare with a second database {#sec-r-second}

For the exercise in [the digression](#sec-second).

### EconBiz

#### How the EconBiz API works

An API (*application programming interface*) is a web address that returns
data instead of a web page. EconBiz has one that is free and needs no key or
account. A search is a single URL:

```text
https://api.econbiz.de/v1/search?q=title:"four-day week"&size=3
```

Paste it into your browser and you see the answer: plain text in the JSON
format, a nested list of fields and values. The URL has three parts that you
can change:

| Parameter | Meaning | Example |
|-----------|---------|---------|
| `q` | the search, in the same syntax as in [the EconBiz section](#sec-econbiz) | `title:"four-day week"` |
| `size` | how many records to return in one answer | `3`, `500` |
| `from` | number of the first record to return, counting from 1 (for paging) | `1`, `501`, `1001` |
| `sort` | order of the records; the default is relevance | `id asc` |

The answer has two parts that matter: `hits` → `total`, the number of hits,
and `hits` → `hits`, the list of records. Each record has fields such as `id`,
`title`, `creator`, `date`, `type` (article, book, …), `source` (ECONIS,
EconStor, RePEc, …), `subject` and `identifier_url` (links, including the DOI
if there is one). The abstract text is **not** included ([see above](#sec-econbiz)). The
list of fields that can appear in an answer
(<https://api.econbiz.de/v1/fields?scope=display>) does name an `abstract`
field, but in our tests (October 2026) it was empty for every record — in the
single-record answers, too.

Which fields you can search is listed under
<https://api.econbiz.de/v1/fields?scope=search>. The list is incomplete:
`abstract` and `description` are missing from it, yet both work in searches.

A single record, with a few more fields such as `language`, has its own
address; the fields come wrapped in an element called `record`:

```text
https://api.econbiz.de/v1/record/10014518487
```

In R, the package [httr2](https://httr2.r-lib.org/) sends the same request.
`req_url_query()` builds the URL for you, including the encoding of spaces and
quotation marks, and `resp_body_json()` turns the answer into an R list:

```{r}
res <- request("https://api.econbiz.de/v1/search") |>
  req_url_query(q = 'title:"four-day week"', size = 3) |>
  req_perform() |>
  resp_body_json()

res$hits$total             # number of hits
length(res$hits$hits)      # records in this answer
res$hits$hits[[1]]$title   # title of the first record
names(res$hits$hits[[1]])  # all fields of the first record
```

The API is a free public service, so use it considerately: count the hits
first, fetch the records once, and save them (as below) instead of sending
the same search again and again. Its terms of use exclude copying the index
at large scale; a review-sized result set is fine. The
[documentation](https://api.econbiz.de/) explains all methods and
parameters. To count without
fetching, ask for `size = 0`: the answer then contains only `total`.

#### The search in R

A small helper puts the same terms into the title, abstract and description
fields ([the EconBiz section](#sec-econbiz) explains why all three):

```{r}
in_fields <- function(terms, fields = c("title", "abstract", "description")) {
  str_c("(", str_c(fields, ":(", terms, ")", collapse = " OR "), ")")
}

work_terms <- '"four-day week" OR "4-day week" OR "four day week"
  OR "working time reduction" OR "work time reduction"
  OR "reduced working hours" OR "shorter working week"'
outcome_terms <- 'productiv* OR well-being OR wellbeing OR satisfaction
  OR burnout OR stress OR absentee* OR turnover OR performance'

eb_query <- str_squish(
  str_c(in_fields(work_terms), " AND ", in_fields(outcome_terms))
)
```

The function below fetches 500 records per request and asks again until it
has all of them. Two details matter: `from` counts from 1, and a fixed sort
order (`id asc`) makes sure that the pages fit together and that a rerun
returns the records in the same order. The function keeps the fields needed
for the comparison, plus the EconStor handle for fetching abstracts. Dates come in mixed formats ("2023", "Oktober 2023",
"26.03.2025"); only the year is kept.

```{r}
econbiz_search <- function(q, page_size = 500) {
  fetch <- function(from) {
    request("https://api.econbiz.de/v1/search") |>
      req_url_query(q = q, size = page_size, from = from, sort = "id asc") |>
      req_perform() |>
      resp_body_json()
  }
  first <- fetch(1)
  hits  <- first$hits$hits
  while (length(hits) < first$hits$total) {
    page <- fetch(length(hits) + 1)$hits$hits
    if (length(page) == 0) break
    hits <- c(hits, page)
  }
  first_or_na <- function(x) if (length(x)) as.character(x[[1]]) else NA_character_
  map(hits, \(x) {
    urls <- unlist(x$identifier_url)
    tibble(
      id     = x$id,
      source = first_or_na(x$source),
      type   = first_or_na(x$type),
      year   = as.integer(str_extract(first_or_na(x$date), "[0-9]{4}")),
      title  = first_or_na(x$title),
      doi    = first_or_na(str_to_lower(str_remove(
                 str_subset(urls, "doi.org/"), ".*doi.org/"))),
      handle = first_or_na(str_extract(urls, "10419/[0-9]+") |> discard(is.na))
    )
  }) |>
    list_rbind()
}

eb <- econbiz_search(eb_query)
write_rds(eb, here("data", str_c("econbiz_", Sys.Date(), ".rds")))
nrow(eb)
```

EconBiz also lists events such as conferences; drop them. Then remove the
duplicates within EconBiz — first by DOI, then by title and year, with the
titles reduced to lower-case letters and digits, because the same work often
comes with slightly different punctuation:

```{r}
eb <- eb |>
  filter(type != "event") |>
  mutate(title_key = str_to_lower(str_remove_all(title, "[^[:alnum:]]"))) |>
  filter(is.na(doi) | !duplicated(doi)) |>
  distinct(title_key, year, .keep_all = TRUE)
nrow(eb)
```

For screening you need the abstracts. Records that link to EconStor get
theirs from EconStor's harvesting interface
(OAI-PMH, a standard way for repositories to share metadata). The answer is
XML, which the package xml2 reads:

```{r}
library(xml2)

econstor_abstract <- function(handle) {
  oai <- request("https://www.econstor.eu/oai/request") |>
    req_url_query(verb = "GetRecord", metadataPrefix = "oai_dc",
                  identifier = str_c("oai:econstor.eu:", handle)) |>
    req_perform() |>
    resp_body_xml()
  abstract <- xml_find_first(oai, ".//dc:description", xml_ns(oai))
  if (inherits(abstract, "xml_missing")) NA_character_ else xml_text(abstract)
}

econstor <- eb |>
  filter(!is.na(handle)) |>
  distinct(handle) |>
  mutate(abstract = map_chr(handle, \(h) {
    Sys.sleep(0.5) # be polite
    econstor_abstract(h)
  }))

eb <- eb |> left_join(econstor, by = "handle")
eb |> summarise(records = n(), with_abstract = sum(!is.na(abstract)))
```

In our example (28 October 2026), this filled in 24 of the 74 abstracts. For
the other records, use the DOI as [with Crossref](#sec-r-abstracts), or the steps for
filling in missing abstracts by hand from step 5.

Now compare with OpenAlex. Records without a DOI cannot be matched this way,
so they are counted separately:

```{r}
oa_dois <- works |> filter(!is.na(doi)) |> pull(doi) |> clean_doi() |> unique()
eb_dois <- eb |> filter(!is.na(doi)) |> pull(doi) |> unique()

c(only_openalex       = length(setdiff(oa_dois, eb_dois)),
  only_econbiz        = length(setdiff(eb_dois, oa_dois)),
  both                = length(intersect(oa_dois, eb_dois)),
  econbiz_without_doi = sum(is.na(eb$doi)))

# What does OpenAlex not find (by DOI)? Kind of publication and source
eb |> filter(!doi %in% oa_dois) |> count(type, source, sort = TRUE)
```

The same function runs the German-language search from [the EconBiz section](#sec-econbiz).
The umlaut in *Arbeitszeitverkürzung* needs an R session in UTF-8. RStudio and
Windows use UTF-8 anyway; if you run R from a terminal and the search returns
far fewer records than expected, check ``l10n_info()$`UTF-8` `` — if it is `FALSE`,
run `Sys.setlocale("LC_CTYPE", "en_US.UTF-8")` first.

```{r}
de_terms <- 'Arbeitszeitverkürzung OR "Vier-Tage-Woche" OR "4-Tage-Woche"'
eb_de <- econbiz_search(in_fields(de_terms))
nrow(eb_de)
```

### Web of Science

If you have access to Web of Science ([see above](#sec-wos)), export the results as a
**tab-delimited file** (record content *Full Record*), save it in
`data/wos/`, and compare by DOI:

```{r}
wos <- list.files(here("data", "wos"), pattern = "\\.txt$", full.names = TRUE) |>
  map(\(f) read_tsv(f, quote = "", col_types = cols(.default = col_character()))) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  distinct(UT, .keep_all = TRUE)

wos_dois <- wos |> filter(!is.na(DI), DI != "") |> pull(DI) |> clean_doi() |> unique()

c(only_openalex = length(setdiff(oa_dois, wos_dois)),
  only_wos      = length(setdiff(wos_dois, oa_dois)),
  both          = length(intersect(oa_dois, wos_dois)))

# Where do the OpenAlex-only records come from?
works |>
  filter(clean_doi(doi) %in% setdiff(oa_dois, wos_dois)) |>
  count(source_display_name, language, sort = TRUE) |>
  head(15)
```

Records without a DOI cannot be matched this way; check a few of them by title.

::: {.callout-tip}
## For the curious: bibliometrics
If you want to go further — co-citation networks, keyword maps, author
collaboration — look at the R package
[bibliometrix](https://www.bibliometrix.org/), which can read OpenAlex data
(`oa2bibliometrix()` in openalexR) as well as Web of Science exports. It is not
needed for the take-home examination.
:::
